item.title: Framing the Eccentrics
item.description: A called strike zone, drawn from enough pitches, is not a crisp rectangle. Its edges are soft — there is a band, an inch or two wide, where a taken pitch is sometimes a ball and sometimes a strike — and the softness is not the same on every side. The boundary is tightest in the upper-inside corner and loosest down and away. A descriptive fit — a binned heatmap, a spline, a boosted-tree model — renders the zone as a lopsided, rounded blob, but much of that shape reflects where pitches are thrown rather than how the umpire calls, and it exaggerates. The truer asymmetry is quieter: not the blob’s outline but the width of the edge itself — sharp in some places, soft in others — which those pictures don’t isolate. More than one perceptual force shapes it, and this paper follows the one with the cleanest signature, the one that tracks something specific: where the umpire is looking.
